title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Saline Township's The Barn data center advances fast—what it means for bills, water and farmland.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Monday morning, August 31, and today we're zeroing in on Saline Township where a big project nicknamed The Barn is moving fast on farmland.
Graham, what's the latest on The Barn itself?

Construction is advancing rapidly right now in Saline Township, according to The Detroit News. Nearby residents are already seeing new power lines going up and more traffic as the facility comes online.
Why is this one moving so quickly compared to others we've heard about?

It looks like the project is pushing ahead even as some local officials tighten zoning rules under pressure. The Detroit News reported it could bring construction jobs but also heavy demands on power and water.
How big are we talking here, and what does that mean for the land?

It's described as a large project on what used to be farmland, so locals are watching land use change fast. Washtenaw County communities are paying close attention to how quickly these builds reshape the area.
And the power side—how does something like this affect electric bills for people living 30 or 60 miles away?

Data centers pull a lot of electricity for cooling and servers. That's one reason DTE asked for a big rate hike earlier this month, and the attorney general pushed back on it. A facility this size adds to that overall demand.
What about water? I keep hearing these places need massive amounts for cooling.

Exactly. Cooling systems can use millions of gallons, and that strains local supplies. Towns are starting to ask hard questions about whether the infrastructure can handle it without raising rates or cutting service elsewhere.
Taxes are another piece, right? How do abatements play into this?

State law lets companies keep the details of those tax breaks secret from residents and local officials. That means towns lose revenue they were counting on, and the rest of us can end up paying more through higher local taxes or strained services.
So even folks far from Saline could feel it in their property taxes or school funding?

That's the concern. When a big project gets big abatements, the township or city has less money coming in, so the burden can shift to everyone else. It's why several communities are pushing for more transparency.
What's the history here—have we seen this pattern before in Michigan?

This is part of a bigger wave. Over the past year or so, places like Ellington Township put a moratorium in place on Saturday to study power and water demands first. Wixom tightened rules on Saturday despite a possible lawsuit.
And Genesee County just got that impact study on Friday. What did it cover?
The panel delivered details on strain to power, water, and roads that could hit taxpayers. Officials there now have concrete numbers to work with before any projects move forward.
How do residents usually find out about these deals if the tax numbers stay hidden?
That's the transparency fight. The Detroit News story today points out that secrecy makes it harder for neighbors to understand exactly how much revenue a township is giving up.
What happens next in Saline specifically?

Construction keeps rolling, new power lines are already visible, and locals will start feeling the traffic and utility changes as it comes online. Other townships are watching to see if they need similar pauses or rules.
Any sense of how many other projects are in the pipeline right now?
Quite a few. Madison Heights filed its first site plan yesterday, and lawmakers in Lansing introduced new state rules on Friday to add oversight on power use, noise, and tax deals.
Those new bills—do they address the secrecy issue we were just talking about?
They aim at tighter oversight overall, including local tax agreements. It's a direct response to the pushback we're seeing in places like Wixom and Ellington.
And the recall effort that failed on Friday—how does that fit the bigger picture?

Voters tried to recall officials who approved rezoning for a big project, but the clerk rejected the petitions. That keeps the 500-acre development moving forward even though the community remains divided.
So the pattern is: proposals advance, communities push back with moratoriums or new rules, and sometimes the projects still move.
That's right. The Saline Barn is the latest example of how quickly things can change once ground is broken.
Graham, let's shift to quick hits. Yesterday Madison Heights got its first data center site plan filing—what does that mean locally?
It's the first concrete step in that Oakland County suburb. If it advances, residents could see added strain on power lines and water systems.
On Saturday, Wixom moved to tighten rules while facing a lawsuit threat. How might that play out?
Officials advanced new restrictions on large projects that draw heavy power and water. Any future campus there could still change taxes, traffic, and utility rates for nearby residents.
Ellington Township also approved a moratorium on Saturday. What's the goal there?
Residents pushed for the pause so the board can study power demands, water use, and tax effects before any big proposals advance. Tuscola County neighbors are watching closely.
Genesee County's impact study landed on Saturday too. What comes next?
Leaders now have the details on potential strain to power, water, and roads. Taxpayers there will want the same level of scrutiny if similar projects pop up nearby.
Friday brought a lot. Attorney General Nessel wants a big cut to DTE's rate hike request.
She told regulators the full $474 million increase would hit households too hard. Data center power demand is one factor behind the ask, so a smaller hike would still mean higher bills for everyone.
New state bills also dropped on Friday targeting big builds.
Lawmakers want fresh rules on power use, noise, and local tax deals. It's a reaction to the growing pushback in communities seeing rapid development.
And the recall effort against officials who approved a massive facility failed on Friday.
Petitions were rejected, so the 500-acre project stays on track even as residents remain split over power use and tax breaks.
Finally today, Michigan is letting data center firms keep tax break details secret.

The Detroit News reported that state law hides those incentives from the public. That reduces transparency on lost revenue for cities and townships, which can mean higher taxes or strained services elsewhere.
Graham, on deck—what meetings can listeners actually attend this week?
No major public hearings are listed for today, but township boards in places like Saline and Wixom are likely to discuss these projects soon.
Should folks check their local clerk's office or township websites for updates?
That's the best move. Agendas often post a few days ahead, especially as more communities weigh moratoriums or new zoning rules.
Anything specific coming up in Genesee or Ellington?
Those boards will probably review the new study and moratorium effects in the next week or two. Worth watching the calendars.
All right, we'll keep tracking that. Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow. Thanks for listening.

episode_title: The Barn Rises in Saline: Power, Water and Tax Shifts Hit Michigan Towns
